clue.text: Fixed small drink extremely daintily

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
tea is the everyday drink

indicators.note: extremely points to the extreme ends of the word daintily, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone takes a small, fixed measure of drink and sips it very delicately.
explanation.definitionFit: Steady describes something firm and unmoving, a direct synonym of fixed as an adjective.

clue.text: Class expert possibly needs single to return in hired vehicle on street

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the word for the hired vehicle

parts.note: a taxi is a vehicle you hire for a journey

indicators.note: to return asks for the word for single to be read backwards

parts.note: mono means single, as in mono sound

explanation.surface: A school class expert needs one person to come back by taxi along the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class' reads as a school form but means a biological category; 'possibly' flags the definition as one example of such an expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who classifies organisms into groups such as genus and species is a specialist in classification.

clue.text: Avoiding sexually indulgent female, initially — what a surprise

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of each of the four words before it

explanation.surface: Someone shocked exclaims at a man steering clear of a promiscuous woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is sarcastic: the exclamation is said when something is not surprising at all, or will never happen.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is an ironic retort of disbelief, much like saying 'fat chance' or a mocking 'what a surprise'.

clue.text: Sign of contempt as cook buys bubbly

indicators.note: bubbly suggests the letters fizzing and moving about, so the words as cook buys are rearranged

explanation.surface: A chef shows scorn by purchasing champagne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bubbly' looks like the champagne the cook buys, but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a childish jeer expressing scorn, a verbal gesture of derision.

clue.text: Article pinned on front of school uniform in exam

indicators.note: pinned on means attached beside, so the pieces sit next to each other in order

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: front of takes the first letter of the word school

parts.note: level means uniform or even throughout

explanation.surface: A badge is pinned to the front of a school uniform during an examination.
explanation.walkthrough: An AS level is an English and Welsh qualification usually taken at about 17, one step below a full A level.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a British school examination, sitting between GCSEs and A levels.

clue.text: Game insubstantial — whisky not required

indicators.note: not required means that letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: wispy means thin and insubstantial, like a wisp of smoke
Whisky is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for the letter W

explanation.surface: A weak game where nobody needs any whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: The children's guessing game where one player names the first letter of something they can see.

clue.text: Out of place, Mike unfortunately punched by rugby player with ball

parts.note: Mike is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for M

indicators.note: punched by means the word is pierced by the following pieces, which go inside it

parts.note: alas is an exclamation meaning unfortunately
a prop is a forward in the front row of a rugby scrum
O resembles a round ball

explanation.surface: Mike is out of position, sadly, after being hit by a rugby player carrying the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' looks like a comment on Mike's bad luck, but it supplies the sigh of regret that gets punched open.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means inappropriate or unsuited to the occasion, taken from French for 'badly to the purpose'.

clue.text: Quiet adult leaving US city

indicators.note: leaving means the letter for adult departs from the city name

parts.note: Seattle is a city in Washington State
A is the film-classification abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: A grown-up quietly quits an American city.
explanation.definitionFit: To calm or soothe someone, as when you get a crying baby to rest; the verb is a synonym of quieten.

clue.text: Help idiot with example, missing the first point

parts.note: an ass is a fool

indicators.note: missing means the compass letter is absent from the word for example

parts.note: an instance is an example
a compass point, here north, N; the first one in the word for example is the one taken

explanation.surface: A plea for help from a fool, whose example has lost its main point.
explanation.walkthrough: INSTANCE has two Ns; 'the first point' says only the first one goes, leaving ISTANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Assistance is aid or support, a straightforward synonym of help as a noun.

clue.text: Mug clasped by the setter wearing blue jewellery in Bow?

indicators.note: wearing means the combined pieces are covered by the word for blue, sitting inside it

parts.note: blue is the colour of the Conservatives, so a Tory

indicators.note: clasped by means the word for mug is held inside the setter's word

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me
a mug is a gullible person, a fool

explanation.surface: A cup held by the setter, who is dressed in blue and wearing jewels in a bow.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is in London's East End, home of Cockney rhyming slang, where 'tom foolery' rhymes with jewellery. 'Bow' looks like a ribbon; it is the place.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cockney rhyming slang the phrase stands for jewels, often shortened to 'tom'.

clue.text: Help found in back of A-to-Z

indicators.note: back of keeps only the rear end of the word for A-to-Z, dropping its front

parts.note: the letters A to Z make up the alphabet

explanation.surface: Help is listed at the back of a street atlas.
explanation.walkthrough: An A-to-Z is also a London street map, which is the surface reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to aid or assist, usually in wrongdoing, as in 'aid and abet'.

clue.text: Silly me left out of aerobatics

indicators.note: out of means the letter for left is taken from the word

parts.note: loops are aerobatic manoeuvres

explanation.surface: Someone berates themself for being dropped from an aerobatics display.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation admits a clumsy mistake, the same as saying 'my mistake' or 'silly me'.

clue.text: Complaint made by others agitated over having impaled vermin

indicators.note: agitated means the letters of others are stirred into a new order
having impaled says the letter for over is stuck through the middle of the word for vermin

parts.note: a rat is a classic piece of vermin
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A complaint from others, worked up over rats being speared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grievance, but it means an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint here is a minor ailment, and an inflamed, painful gullet is one.

clue.text: European in glider, his flying trip in Alaska?

indicators.note: in places the European letter inside the rearranged letters
flying suggests the letters of glider and his being thrown about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A European in his glider takes an airborne trip over Alaska.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows the definition is by example: Alaska is simply a snowy place where such a trip is likely.
explanation.definitionFit: In a snowy place such as Alaska an outing might be a journey on a horse- or dog-drawn sledge.

clue.text: Gear lifted by thugs, namely, infiltrating American organisation

indicators.note: lifted in a down clue means the word for gear is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: rig is gear or equipment

indicators.note: infiltrating means the abbreviation for namely gets inside the word for thugs

parts.note: louts are rough, aggressive men
sc. abbreviates scilicet, Latin for namely

explanation.surface: Equipment stolen by thugs, who have got inside an American organisation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' reads as stolen, but in a down clue it means turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the youth movement for girls in the USA, the counterpart of Britain's Guides.

clue.text: Quarrel very loudly in terrible decree nisi — not half

indicators.note: in means the musical letters go inside the rearranged letters
terrible means the letters are in a terrible mess and need reordering
not half means only half the word nisi is kept, its first two letters

parts.note: ff, fortissimo, is the musical direction for very loud

explanation.surface: A furious row in a divorce case over a dreadful provisional decree.
explanation.walkthrough: A decree nisi is a provisional divorce order in England; the anagram leaves the letters DIERENCE before the musical letters go in.
explanation.definitionFit: A difference can be a disagreement or argument, as in 'settle our differences'.

clue.text: Brother attending holy church by which you might march down Caledonian Road?

definitions.text: by which you might march down Caledonian Road?

indicators.note: attending means accompanying, so the pieces stand beside each other

parts.note: pi is a slang shortening of pious, holy

explanation.surface: A monk going to church, perhaps the one on a Scottish road.
explanation.walkthrough: Caledonia is Scotland; Caledonian Road is in London, but the 'road' here is the Scottish one. 'holy' gives PI, a crossword shortening of pious.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a piece of Highland bagpipe music, the kind a piper might play while marching through Scotland.

clue.text: Decline theatre cancellation by doctor?

indicators.note: by means beside, so the pieces sit next to each other

parts.note: an op, an operation, takes place in an operating theatre
off means cancelled, as in 'the match is off'

explanation.surface: A doctor calling off a show in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' reads as a playhouse, but it is the operating theatre, giving OP.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop-off is a fall or decrease, as in a drop-off in sales, so it means a decline.

clue.text: Books found in river — English course

indicators.note: found in means the books' abbreviation lies inside the river's name

parts.note: the Aire is a river in Yorkshire
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Books are discovered in a river on an English golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: Aintree, near Liverpool, is the racecourse where the Grand National is run.
explanation.definitionFit: A course here is a racecourse, and this is the famous one on Merseyside.

clue.text: Tabulated facts first seen in branch of mechanics

indicators.note: seen in means the abbreviation for first appears inside the word for the branch of mechanics

parts.note: statics is the branch of mechanics dealing with bodies at rest
1st, written with the letter I for the figure 1, means first

explanation.surface: Data tables were first observed in a field of physics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' gives 1ST, with the figure 1 read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Numerical data collected and arranged in tables is what the word denotes.

clue.text: Private party admitting soldiers

indicators.note: admitting means letting the soldiers' abbreviation inside the word for party

parts.note: a sect is a faction or party
RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: A private party lets some soldiers in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' reads as an army rank beside 'soldiers', but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Something kept secret is confidential and hidden, the adjective sense of private.

clue.text: Company boss originally kept inside an island hut

indicators.note: inside says that opening letter goes within the abbreviation for the boss

parts.note: SEO abbreviates senior executive officer, a company boss

indicators.note: originally takes the opening letter of the word kept

explanation.surface: A company chief, at first, was kept inside an island hut.
explanation.walkthrough: A skeo is a hut used for drying fish or meat in Orkney and Shetland.
explanation.definitionFit: This rare Scottish-islands word names a stone drying shed, the hut of the definition.

clue.text: Husband getting a lift, perhaps daily

indicators.note: getting here means getting into, so the husband's letter goes inside the vehicle

parts.note: a car can give someone a lift, a ride

explanation.surface: A husband is given a lift, maybe every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' looks like an adverb, but it is a noun: a daily is a British cleaner who comes in each day.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a char, or charwoman, is a cleaning lady, also called a daily.

clue.text: Bliss, maybe of troubled star Monroe

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed, so the letters of star Monroe are rearranged

explanation.surface: A happy moment, perhaps, for the troubled film star Marilyn Monroe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bliss' looks like happiness, but it is Nathaniel Bliss, an 18th-century Astronomer Royal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nathaniel Bliss held the post of Astronomer Royal, so he is one example of a stargazing scientist.

clue.text: Thank heavens it contains sign of life!

indicators.note: it contains says the letters are held within the words Thank heavens

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims with relief at spotting a sign of life.
explanation.definitionFit: This Egyptian hieroglyph, a looped cross, symbolises life.

clue.text: Regulars in Boer War imprisoning cold killer

indicators.note: imprisoning means those letters lock the cold letter inside them
regulars in takes every other letter of the words Boer War, starting with the second

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Regular soldiers in the Boer War lock up a cold-blooded killer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regulars' looks like regular troops, but it picks every second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The killer whale is the common name for this black-and-white marine predator.

clue.text: Rely on me backing police to seal north London station

indicators.note: on means the word for rely comes after the reversed word
backing means the word me is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
to bank on something is to rely on it, so bank means rely

indicators.note: to seal means the police word closes round the north letter

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: Trust me to support the police in sealing off a north London station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns ME into EM. Embankment is a London Underground station by the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Embankment is a Tube station in central London, beside the riverside road of the same name.

clue.text: Splits fish netted by ship

indicators.note: netted by means the fish is caught inside the abbreviation for ship

parts.note: SS stands for steamship
hake is a fish

explanation.surface: A fish is caught in the net of a ship and broken apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Splits' is a verb: Chambers gives 'split' as a sense of the transitive verb shake, as timber cracks.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber that develops cracks is said to shake, so the verb sense matches splitting or cracking.
